# Worksheet: a thousand people, and what the average hides

**~45 minutes**

The [chapter](../../chapters/06-agent-based-models.qmd) built a well-mixed SIR
model out of a thousand named individuals and compared it with the ODE. This
worksheet takes the same model and asks two questions the chapter raises but does
not settle: what does the timestep $\Delta t$ do, and what does the
deterministic model fail to see?

Every other session this week has been a population model, where the state is a
few numbers. This one is different in kind: the state is a thousand people, and
the population curves are something you compute *afterwards*.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Part C is the point of the session**, and it is the one that connects back to
the jump-process session on Day 2. Parts A and B are quick; do not let Part B's
figure absorb the time that C needs. Worked solutions are posted at the end of
each day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

::: {.callout-note}
`Δt` here is not a solver tolerance. In the ODE sessions the timestep was a
numerical detail the solver chose and refined until it stopped mattering. In this
model `Δt` is part of the *model definition*: it sets how many contacts a person
makes per step and how often anyone can recover. Part B is about what follows
from that.
:::

---

## Setup

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-setup
using Agents
using CairoMakie
using Distributions
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

const N = 1000
const β = 0.05
const c = 10.0
const γ = 0.25
const horizon = 40.0

@agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
    next_status::Symbol
end

println("R₀ = ", β * c / γ)
```

Each `Person` carries two statuses, not one. That is deliberate, and Part A's
first question asks why.

---

## Part A — the rules, written as an agent (~12 min)

An agent-based model is defined by what one individual does in one step. Two
things happen to a person: a susceptible makes some contacts and may be infected
by one of them, and an infectious person may recover.

Both need a *rate* turned into a *probability over a step of length $\Delta t$*.
The contact side is given to you: a susceptible draws
$K\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\,\Delta t)$ contacts, each of which transmits with
probability $\beta$ if the person contacted happens to be infectious. Your two
`# TODO`s are the recovery probability and the commit step.

For recovery, the waiting time is exponential with rate $\gamma$, exactly as in
the jump-process session. The probability of having recovered by the end of one
step is therefore $1-e^{-\gamma\Delta t}$.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a1
function agent_step!(person, model)
    person.next_status = person.status
    if person.status == :S
        for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt))
            contact = random_agent(model)
            if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β
                person.next_status = :I
                break
            end
        end
    elseif person.status == :I
        # TODO: recover with probability 1 - exp(-γ Δt) over this step
        if rand(abmrng(model)) < 0.0
            person.next_status = :R
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

function model_step!(model)
    for person in allagents(model)
        # TODO: commit the status each agent decided on during this step
    end
    return nothing
end

susceptible_count(model) = count(p.status == :S for p in allagents(model))
infected_count(model) = count(p.status == :I for p in allagents(model))
recovered_count(model) = count(p.status == :R for p in allagents(model))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A, the two rules

```julia
if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt)
```

and, inside the `model_step!` loop:

```julia
person.status = person.next_status
```

`abmrng(model)` is the model's own random stream — using it rather than a global
`rand()` is what makes a seeded run reproducible. If the epidemic never gets
going, check the commit line: without it, nobody's status ever changes.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a2
function initialize_model(seed; I0 = 10, Δt = 0.1)
    model = StandardABM(
        Person;
        agent_step!,
        model_step!,
        properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt),
        rng = StableRNG(seed),
    )
    for id in 1:N
        status = id <= I0 ? :I : :S
        add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status = status), model)
    end
    return model
end

function simulate(seed; I0 = 10, Δt = 0.1)
    steps = round(Int, horizon / Δt)
    _, data = run!(
        initialize_model(seed; I0, Δt),
        steps;
        mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count],
        showprogress = false,
    )
    return Matrix(data[:, [
        :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count,
    ]])'
end

single_run = simulate(20250711)
step_times = collect(0.0:0.1:horizon)

check("every person has exactly one status at every step",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(single_run; dims = 1)) .- N)) == 0)
check("counts are whole people and never negative", minimum(single_run) >= 0)
check("the epidemic took off", single_run[3, end] > 100)

(; final_counts = single_run[:, end],
   peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]),
   peak_time = step_times[argmax(single_run[2, :])])
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-a3
function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t)
    b, contact, g, n = p
    infection = b * contact * u[1] * u[2] / n
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - g * u[2]
    du[3] = g * u[2]
    return nothing
end

ode_solution = solve(
    ODEProblem(sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, horizon), (β, c, γ, N)),
    Tsit5(); saveat = step_times,
)
ode_states = Array(ode_solution)

(; abm_peak = maximum(single_run[2, :]),
   ode_peak = round(maximum(ode_states[2, :]); digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-single
#| fig-cap: "One individual-based realization (steps) against the deterministic SIR trajectory (dashed)."
fig = Figure(size = (820, 450))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people",
          title = "One realization, N = 1000")
for (j, (name, colour)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"],
                                         [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen]))
    stairs!(ax, step_times, single_run[j, :]; color = colour, linewidth = 2,
            label = "$name (ABM)")
    lines!(ax, step_times, ode_states[j, :]; color = colour, linestyle = :dash,
           linewidth = 1.5, label = "$name (ODE)")
end
axislegend(ax; position = :rc, nbanks = 2)
fig
```

### A1. Interpret

- `agent_step!` writes to `next_status` and `model_step!` copies it across
  afterwards. Suppose it wrote to `person.status` directly instead. What could
  then happen within a single step that should not, and what would the answer
  start to depend on?
- The recovery probability could have been written `γ * Δt`, which is simpler.
  At $\Delta t = 0.1$ how much difference would that make, and at what value of
  $\Delta t$ does it stop being defensible at all?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part B — the timestep is a modelling choice (~15 min)

Holding physical time fixed at 40 units, coarsen and refine $\Delta t$ and see
what happens. Sixteen seeded replicates per value keeps this quick; the standard
error is reported so you can tell a real shift from scatter.

The quantity below is the **mean of the replicate peaks**, $\frac1n\sum_r\max_t
I_r(t)$: each run's own maximum, averaged. That is not the same as the peak of
the averaged curve, and the second cell in this part is about the difference.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b1
replicate_seeds = 4000 .+ (1:16)
timesteps = (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0)

standard_error(x) = std(x) / sqrt(length(x))
ode_peak = maximum(ode_states[2, :])

# TODO: the peak infectious count from each replicate, for each Δt in turn
peaks_by_dt = [[0.0 for seed in replicate_seeds] for Δt in timesteps]

peak_summary = map(zip(timesteps, peaks_by_dt)) do (Δt, peaks)
    (Δt = Δt,
     mean_of_replicate_peaks = round(mean(peaks); digits = 1),
     se = round(standard_error(peaks); digits = 1),
     difference_from_ode = round(mean(peaks) - ode_peak; digits = 1))
end
```

Deciding whether two timesteps differ needs the uncertainty of the *difference*,
not of either mean alone. Reusing the same seed numbers is not enough to call
the two sets independent, since they are driven by the same random streams.
Rather than assume anything about how they are related, take the difference
replicate by replicate and find the standard error of that.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b1-checks
function difference(i, j)
    per_replicate = peaks_by_dt[i] .- peaks_by_dt[j]
    (; mean_difference = mean(per_replicate),
       se = standard_error(per_replicate))
end

coarse = difference(5, 2)   # Δt = 1.0 against 0.1
fine = difference(1, 2)     # Δt = 0.05 against 0.1

check("coarsening to Δt = 1 inflates the peak well beyond the scatter",
      coarse.mean_difference > 4 * coarse.se)
check("refining from 0.1 to 0.05 does not resolve a difference",
      abs(fine.mean_difference) < 3 * fine.se)

(; coarse = map(x -> round(x; digits = 2), coarse),
   fine = map(x -> round(x; digits = 2), fine))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b1-table
peak_summary
```

`difference_from_ode` is not called a bias. It mixes three things:
the timestep effect, the upward pull of averaging maxima, and finite-population
noise. To isolate the timestep alone, remove the randomness and iterate
the deterministic mean-field map, which uses the identical frozen-within-a-step
update rule. Any distance between it and the ODE is discretization error and
nothing else.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b1-map
function mean_field_peak(Δt; S = 990.0, I = 10.0)
    peak = I
    for _ in 1:round(Int, horizon / Δt)
        new_infections = S * (1 - exp(-c * β * Δt * I / N))
        new_recoveries = I * (1 - exp(-γ * Δt))
        S -= new_infections
        I += new_infections - new_recoveries
        peak = max(peak, I)
    end
    return peak
end

[(; Δt, map_peak = round(mean_field_peak(Δt); digits = 1),
    timestep_error = round(mean_field_peak(Δt) - ode_peak; digits = 1))
 for Δt in timesteps]
```

Read that table against the ensemble one. The map says $\Delta t=0.25$ already
carries roughly a ten-person upward error, yet sixteen replicates cannot see it.
Failing to resolve a difference is not the same as showing there is none.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B, the sweep

```julia
peaks_by_dt = [[maximum(simulate(seed; Δt)[2, :]) for seed in replicate_seeds]
               for Δt in timesteps]
```

`simulate` already converts `Δt` into the right number of steps, so physical time
stays fixed at 40 for every value. Row 2 is $I$. Keeping the peaks themselves,
rather than only their means, is what lets the next cell difference them
replicate by replicate.
:::

Now a second question, which is about the *summary* rather than the timestep. At
$\Delta t = 0.1$, compare the average of the individual peaks with the peak of
the averaged trajectory. These sound like the same quantity.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-b2
ensemble = cat((simulate(seed) for seed in replicate_seeds)...; dims = 3)
mean_trajectory = dropdims(mean(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3)

individual_peaks = [maximum(ensemble[2, :, k]) for k in axes(ensemble, 3)]
individual_peak_times = [step_times[argmax(ensemble[2, :, k])]
                         for k in axes(ensemble, 3)]

mean_of_peaks = mean(individual_peaks)
peak_of_mean = maximum(mean_trajectory[2, :])

check("the mean of the peaks is above the ODE peak", mean_of_peaks > ode_peak)
check("the peak of the mean trajectory is below it", peak_of_mean < ode_peak)

(; mean_of_peaks = round(mean_of_peaks; digits = 1),
   ode_peak = round(ode_peak; digits = 1),
   peak_of_mean = round(peak_of_mean; digits = 1),
   peak_time_range = extrema(individual_peak_times))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-timestep
#| fig-cap: "Left: mean of the replicate peaks against timestep, with standard-error bars, the ODE peak dashed and the deterministic-map peak in grey. Right: sixteen realizations at Δt = 0.1, their pointwise mean, and the ODE."
fig = Figure(size = (980, 430))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Δt", ylabel = "mean of replicate peaks",
           xscale = log10, title = "Coarser steps, bigger epidemic")
errorbars!(ax1, collect(timesteps),
           [s.mean_of_replicate_peaks for s in peak_summary],
           [s.se for s in peak_summary]; whiskerwidth = 10, color = :black)
scatterlines!(ax1, collect(timesteps),
              [s.mean_of_replicate_peaks for s in peak_summary];
              color = :darkorange, markersize = 10, label = "replicate peaks")
scatterlines!(ax1, collect(timesteps), [mean_field_peak(Δt) for Δt in timesteps];
              color = :slategrey, marker = :diamond, markersize = 9,
              linestyle = :dot, label = "deterministic map")
hlines!(ax1, [ode_peak]; color = :grey, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax1, 0.06, ode_peak - 12; text = "ODE peak", fontsize = 12, color = :grey)
axislegend(ax1; position = :lt)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious people",
           title = "Averaging smears the peak")
for k in axes(ensemble, 3)
    lines!(ax2, step_times, ensemble[2, :, k]; color = (:steelblue, 0.35),
           linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax2, step_times, mean_trajectory[2, :]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3,
       label = "ensemble mean")
lines!(ax2, step_times, ode_states[2, :]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash,
       linewidth = 2, label = "ODE")
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt)
fig
```

### B1. Interpret

- Read the `peak_summary` table against the *combined* standard errors. Over
  which range of $\Delta t$ can you resolve no difference at all, and where does
  the effect become undeniable? Now put the deterministic-map table beside it:
  at $\Delta t = 0.25$, does the ensemble's silence mean the timestep error is
  small, or only that sixteen replicates cannot see it? Write the conclusion you
  would be willing to defend.
- Is the coarsening effect numerical error, a changed biological assumption, or
  both? Think about what a single agent can and cannot observe within one step.
- `mean_of_peaks` is above the ODE peak and `peak_of_mean` is below it, from the
  same sixteen runs. Using `peak_time_range`, explain how both can be true, and
  say which one you would give to someone sizing a hospital ward.

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — what an average hides completely (~15 min)

Everything so far started with ten infectious people, where the epidemic is
essentially certain to take off. Real outbreaks start with one. The ODE cannot
represent what then happens, because a fractional person still transmits.

Two hundred introductions of a single case, each with its own seed. Your `# TODO`
is to classify the outcomes: an outbreak that never got going, against one that
did.

A *final* size means the epidemic has finished. Stopping the clock at
$t = 40$ would not do that here, because over half of these runs are still
infectious then. `final_size` runs each model until nobody is infectious and
returns the recovered count at that point.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c1
#| error: true
introduction_seeds = 9000 .+ (1:200)

function final_size(seed; I0 = 1, Δt = 0.1, max_steps = 2000)
    model = initialize_model(seed; I0, Δt)
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model)
        step!(model, 1)
    end
    error("epidemic still infectious after $max_steps steps; increase max_steps " *
          "(if Part A's model_step! is still unfinished, complete that first)")
end

final_sizes = [final_size(seed) for seed in introduction_seeds]

# TODO: true for the runs that fizzled out — use a cutoff of 100 total infections
fizzled = falses(length(final_sizes))
fizzle_fraction = mean(fizzled)
theoretical_extinction = γ / (β * c)

both_groups_present = any(fizzled) && !all(fizzled)
split_is_clean = both_groups_present &&
                 maximum(final_sizes[fizzled]) < 100 &&
                 minimum(final_sizes[.!fizzled]) > 100

check("the outcome is sharply bimodal, so the cutoff is not delicate",
      split_is_clean)
check("the fizzle fraction is close to 1/R₀",
      abs(fizzle_fraction - theoretical_extinction) < 0.1)

(; fizzle_fraction, theoretical_extinction, split_is_clean,
   largest_fizzle = both_groups_present ? maximum(final_sizes[fizzled]) : nothing,
   smallest_takeoff = both_groups_present ? minimum(final_sizes[.!fizzled]) : nothing)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C, classifying outcomes

```julia
fizzled = final_sizes .< 100
```

The dot makes the comparison element by element, giving a vector of
`true`/`false`. `.!fizzled` then negates it element by element, which is how the
checks pick out the runs that took off.
:::

A cutoff you chose yourself can manufacture the split it claims to find, so
check that it sits in an empty range rather than cutting through data.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c1b
#| error: true
[(; cutoff,
    fizzle_fraction = round(mean(final_sizes .< cutoff); digits = 3),
    conditional_mean = round(mean(final_sizes[final_sizes .>= cutoff]); digits = 1))
 for cutoff in (20, 50, 100, 200, 400)]
```

The ODE needs the same treatment: at $t = 40$ it still has more than fifty
infectious people, so `horizon` is nowhere near its final size either. Integrate
it far enough out that $I$ has effectively vanished.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c2
ode_single_introduction = solve(
    ODEProblem(sir_drift!, [999.0, 1.0, 0.0], (0.0, 400.0), (β, c, γ, N)),
    Tsit5(),
)
ode_final_size = ode_single_introduction.u[end][3]

(; I_at_horizon = round(ode_single_introduction(horizon)[2]; digits = 1),
   R_at_horizon = round(ode_single_introduction(horizon)[3]; digits = 1),
   R_asymptotic = round(ode_final_size; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch06-c2b
#| error: true
unconditional_mean = mean(final_sizes)
conditional_mean = mean(final_sizes[.!fizzled])

check("the ODE is nothing like the average outcome",
      abs(unconditional_mean - ode_final_size) > 200)
check("the ODE does describe the epidemics that take off",
      abs(conditional_mean - ode_final_size) < 30)

(; unconditional_mean = round(unconditional_mean; digits = 1),
   conditional_mean = round(conditional_mean; digits = 1),
   ode_final_size = round(ode_final_size; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch06-extinction
#| error: true
#| fig-cap: "Final epidemic size across 200 introductions of a single infectious person, with the ODE prediction and the mean over all runs marked."
fig = Figure(size = (860, 430))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "final number recovered", ylabel = "runs",
          title = "200 single-case introductions, R₀ = 2")
hist!(ax, Float64.(final_sizes); bins = 40, color = (:steelblue, 0.8))
vlines!(ax, [ode_final_size]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2,
        label = "ODE prediction")
vlines!(ax, [unconditional_mean]; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2,
        label = "mean over all runs")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### C1. Interpret

- The fizzle fraction lands near $1/R_0$. Recall the branching-process argument
  from the jump-process session and say why that value, and why the depletion of
  susceptibles does not spoil it. Note that $1/R_0 = 0.5$ is the *continuous-time*
  answer; this model takes synchronous steps of $\Delta t = 0.1$, so its own
  branching approximation gives about $0.488$ instead. With 200 runs, can you
  tell those two apart?
- The ODE's asymptotic final size is about 797. The average ABM outcome is
  nowhere near it, yet the average *among the runs that took off* matches it
  closely. Write the one-sentence statement of what the ODE is a good model of.
- The red line in the figure — the mean over all runs — falls in the empty gap
  between the two modes. What does that say about reporting a mean here?
- Parts A and B started from ten cases and showed none of this. Why did the
  effect disappear, and what does that tell you about when an individual-level
  model is worth its cost?

> *Your answer here.*
